_note: Per-assembly coverage floors, enforced by scripts/coverage-gate.ps1 on PRs and on main. A null floor is not enforced — the assembly is reported and passed. Setting a number is the whole act of turning the gate on for that assembly, and it is deliberately the only thing anyone has to edit.
_scope: Domain and Application only, per the plan. Api, Web, Worker and Infrastructure are report-only forever unless that is revisited in writing: their coverage is dominated by wiring and by code whose value is not proven by line count. There is deliberately no solution-wide aggregate floor — an aggregate lets a collapse in one assembly hide behind a rise in another.
_settingThem: Floors start a couple of points BELOW observed reality, so ordinary variance does not fail an unrelated PR. Ratcheting up when a trend holds is a normal PR. Never ratchet down without writing why in the same commit. The observed range is in history.json on the coverage-history branch; scripts/coverage-gate.ps1 -Suggest prints it against the current floors.
_set: Floors set 2026-08-07, earlier than the plan's ~two weeks, because the wait was for evidence of volatility and the evidence already exists. Across 78 recorded runs and both coverage engines, the largest movement in any of these four numbers is 0.4 points: old engine (64 runs, 08-01 to 08-05, spanning features, dependency bumps that widened analyzers, and a test scrub that deleted 21 cases) moved Domain line 0.1, Domain branch 0.0, Application line 0.4, Application branch 0.3; new engine (14 runs) moved 0.0, 0.0, 0.2, 0.0. The engine change reset the absolute values but not the volatility, and volatility is what a floor has to survive. A 2-point margin is five times the largest movement ever recorded.
_basis: Each floor is 2 points under the MINIMUM observed on the current engine, not under the latest run — scripts/coverage-gate.ps1 -Suggest reads one run and says so itself. Minima: Domain 98.8/97.6, Application 94.4/84.2.
_enforcement_now: enforcement stays 'alert' with these first numbers on purpose: a floor that has never been observed failing is a claim, and the first thing to learn is whether it ever fires under ordinary work. Flip to 'gate' once it has been quiet through a few weeks of real changes. Note before flipping: ci.yml is on: pull_request and this repo pushes straight to main, so a gate would only ever be evaluated after the deploy unless deploy is made to need the coverage job.
_enforcement: What a breach DOES, kept next to the numbers so one file answers both 'what is the floor' and 'what happens when we miss it'. 'alert' reports a breach as a warning and lets the run continue; 'gate' fails it. This is not the same knob as a null floor: null means the assembly is not measured against anything, alert means it is measured and the answer is published without stopping work. A missing assembly stays fatal in both modes — that is not a coverage judgment, it is the gate reporting on nothing, and there is no reading of it that should be a warning.
